newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. funds batter Singapore dollar - dealers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. funds batter Singapore dollar - dealers.

text.p: The Singapore dollar, traditionally a safe haven during Southeast Asian currency volatility, came under attack on Thursday from U.S. funds, dealers said.
It continued to slide in late afternoon trading as the U.S. funds tested its "safe-haven" status and interest rates in the city state fell.

By 1100 GMT, the Singapore dollar was trading around 1.4343/53 to the dollar compared to about 1.4300 on Wednesday. "The further weakness in the afternoon is basically because the Singapore interest rates came off," a dealer with a local bank told Reuters.
Singapore's overnight interbank rate declined to around two percent on Thursday against 2-11/16 percent on Wednesday.
Dealers said U.S. funds continued to test how low Singapore's currency could go against the U.S. dollar.
Buying from various parties emerged after the Singapore dollar broke 1.4315/20 to the dollar and stop-losses were triggered.
"U.S. funds are still buying the dollar against the Sing. At this rate, I think we could see the Sing going to 1.4355 to the dollar soon," said another dealer with a U.S. bank.
"People think the Singapore dollar won't be attacked because of its safe-haven reputation. But these U.S. funds are testing this reputation," a dealer with a European bank said.
"All the Americans want to do is to test the various stops to see how low the Sing dollar would go. They want to see how the weak shorts will be triggered out," he said.
Dealers said the U.S. dollar rose against the local currency after a British party emerged to buy on behalf of some U.S. funds from 1.4310 onwards.
"The Americans were buying the dollar against the Sing since late New York last night and they are just continuing to test all the stops," a dealer with a U.S. bank said.
He said the first stop at 1.4320 was tested and triggered and now U.S. funds were looking to test the next resistance at 1.4355.
Some dealers said the Singapore currency's "safe-haven" reputation was fairly vulnerable this time due to a weak stock market and an economy whose growth has slowed.

"Previously, the Singapore dollar, with the strong economy, was seen as a good buy every time something bad happens in the region. It's not so now. I would tend to be neutral on the Singapore dollar," said the dealer with the European bank.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Singapore's de facto central bank, does intervene in the open market but it usually does not comment on its position.
MAS officials were not immediately available for comment.
In its annual report issued earlier this week, the MAS said it expected the Singapore dollar's modest rate of appreciation to continue.
